claims.text: Silver is a low-melting, lubricious phase suitable for microalloying CoCrFeNi.
Adding silver to CoCrFeNi will enable in-situ formation of a self-adaptive lubricious surface layer during sliding.
The Ag-modified alloy will maintain low friction and wear from room temperature to 800 °C.
An approximately 2 wt% Ag addition can be uniformly distributed in the CoCrFeNi matrix during synthesis.
Mechanical and thermal stimuli during sliding will cause silver to segregate to the contact surface.
The segregated silver will form a continuous silver-rich surface film.
The silver-rich surface film will act as a dynamic self-lubricant across the specified temperature range.
At lower temperatures, Ag will remain largely stable within the CoCrFeNi matrix.
At elevated temperatures, especially above approximately 700 °C, Ag diffusion and surface segregation will accelerate.
A silver-rich interfacial film will lower interfacial shear strength.
Lower interfacial shear strength from the silver-rich film will reduce friction and wear.
Unmodified CoCrFeNi tends to exhibit increased friction and wear during high-temperature sliding.
Relative to unmodified CoCrFeNi, the Ag-modified alloy will have both a lower coefficient of friction and a lower wear rate throughout room temperature to 800 °C.
The predicted benefit applies in ambient air under a constant load and controlled sliding speed.
Changing atmosphere, mechanical load, or strain rate could alter the effectiveness of the Ag intervention.

contradictions.description: The mechanism claims that the lubricating film remains effective as load and environmental conditions vary, whereas the experiment holds those variables constant and the boundary states that changing them could affect effectiveness.
